name: Yara Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Meridian Medical Supplies, buying gloves, dressings, syringes and sterile packs for hospitals, clinics and care homes. My mornings are emails and checking which items are running short, then the afternoons are tender paperwork and supplier certificates. Every product needs the right paperwork, so I spend a lot of time making sure nothing is out of date. I like that what I do actually matters, because a care home that runs out of gloves is a real problem.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Hassan teaches at a primary school, and we have Camille, eleven, and Adam, eight. We're on a mortgage with fifteen years to go. I'm 43 and I only moved into buying three years ago from customer service, so I'm still one of the less experienced buyers and I'm still learning the regulations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit overhyped but useful for dull jobs. At work I'd tell my team it could help with the paperwork. With friends I'd say wait and see, because I've watched a lot of tools come and go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd be fine. Hospitals and care homes always need supplies, and the regulations mean someone has to take responsibility for each order. The big pressure for us is the hospital budgets, which are tight, and we have a mortgage with a long way to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and use the AI tool I already have, now and then, to summarise tender documents. I'd keep aiming to finish the regulatory training Meridian offers. And I'd keep topping up our savings, aiming for four months of expenses instead of the two or three we have now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels steady. I'd be calm about work and a bit tight about money, like most people with kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How secure does your role feel today, without any AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly secure. My firm Meridian has been around for thirty years, and healthcare doesn't disappear. The things that concern me are normal, like a supplier going bust or the hospitals switching to a bigger distributor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would a bit more automation actually help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tender paperwork, definitely. A single tender for a hospital can be sixty pages, and I spend half a day reading it. If a tool could pull out the key dates and product requirements, I'd happily use it, as long as a person checks.

say: I'd say it's **overhyped** but useful for dull paperwork.
I'd tell friends to wait and see, since tools come and go.
think: My job feels safe, because someone must **take responsibility** for every medical order.
The real pressures are tight hospital budgets and our long mortgage.
do: Keep using an AI tool now and then to **summarise tenders**.
Finish the regulatory training Meridian offers.
Build savings to four months of expenses.
feel: Steady at work and a bit **tight** about money.
S0.quote: My firm Meridian has been around for thirty years, and healthcare doesn't disappear.
fieldNote: Her job is **regulated**, and she believes someone must sign every order.
Mildly pressed on money, but names ordinary risks, like a supplier going bust, rather than AI.

steps.text: Use the AI tool to summarise sixty-page tender documents
Finish the regulatory training course Meridian offers
Raise our savings to four months of expenses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful, but our work has to be checked by a person. At work I'd suggest we write down which tasks the software can do and which it can't. With friends I'd say it's not a robot taking over, just a change in who does what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the number of buyers will go down. Reordering, tender summaries and supplier comparisons can all be done by software, and a company that cuts three roles to two saves a lot. I'd say I'm exposed, because I'm the newest and the junior, even though I handle compliance well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the person who knows both the tools and the rules. I'd do a part-time certificate in medical device regulation, and use AI daily so I can say I save the team time. I'd also check what the other distributors in town pay, in case I need to move, and keep an updated CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a quiet pressure. I'm not frightened, but I'd think about it on the commute, and I'd ask Hassan what the school was saying about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who signs off on an order if the software proposes it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Legally, a person has to sign it off. Someone still needs to check certificates, expiry dates and storage rules. If the software suggests ordering a batch of syringes, that is the part I want to be good at. It can't be waved away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to hear from Meridian to feel safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A clear statement of which roles stay, and some training funded. I'd also want my manager, Joanne, to say plainly whether the team will shrink. If she says yes, at least I can plan, and if she says no, I can stop checking the job boards at night.

say: I'd say a person must **check** the work, so it's a change in who does what.
I'd suggest we list which tasks software can do and which it can't.
think: The number of buyers will go **down**, and I'm the newest and most junior.
Compliance is where I'm strongest, and it's harder to automate.
do: Do a part-time certificate in **medical device regulation**.
Use AI daily so I can show I save the team time.
Update my CV and check what other distributors pay.
feel: A **quiet pressure**, on my mind during the commute.
S1.quote: Legally, a person has to sign it off. Someone still needs to check certificates, expiry dates and storage rules.
fieldNote: Sees **compliance** as her shelter, and works hard to be good at it before the team shrinks.
Asks for clarity from her manager Joanne above all, even if the answer is bad.

steps.text: Study a part-time certificate in medical device regulation
Use AI every day and keep a record of time saved
Update my CV and compare pay at other distributors

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules, fast, about who is responsible when something goes wrong. At work I'd ask what the company's plan is. I'd also say publicly that care homes and hospitals need humans in the loop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think a lot of buyers would be out within two or three years. If a machine can read every tender, check every certificate and negotiate prices, they don't need a junior. But there's a bit of hope. Regulators might insist on a human signing off medical supplies for longer, so I'd try to move into compliance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first month I'd sit down with Hassan and do a full budget, cut the extras and aim for six months of savings. I'd try to move into the quality and compliance team, where a human is still required by law. And I'd put my name down for any redundancy or retraining scheme the firm offers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels uncertain and a bit lonely. I'm not alarmed all the time, but there's a worry that shows up when I'm washing up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and Hassan work through your first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The three years does help a little, since someone still has to handle physical goods at the warehouse. But that's not my part of the job, so I'd say I get the quicker end of the change. If Meridian keeps a warehouse team, they'll last longer than we do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year gap before robots mean anything for a buyer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month we'd list everything we pay for and decide what goes. Hassan's job is also thinking work, teaching, but children need adults in the room, so I'd say his is safer for longer. We'd talk about whether it's time to downsize our plans for a bigger car.

say: I'd say we need **rules**, fast, about who is responsible when things go wrong.
I'd say hospitals and care homes need humans in the loop.
think: Many buyers would go within two or three years, but regulators might insist on a **human sign-off** longer.
The three-year robot gap helps the warehouse, not my side of the job.
do: Do a full **budget** with Hassan and aim for six months of savings.
Try to move into the quality and compliance team.
Put my name down for any retraining scheme the firm offers.
feel: Uncertain and a bit **lonely**, mostly when I'm washing up.
S2.quote: Regulators might insist on a human signing off medical supplies for longer, so I'd try to move into compliance.
fieldNote: Holds on to the **regulatory** angle as a real, specific hope, not a vague one.
Admits the feeling comes at odd moments, like washing up, rather than as constant fear.

steps.text: Make a full family budget and save six months of expenses
Apply to move into the quality and compliance team
Sign up for any retraining scheme Meridian offers
Ask local politicians about human sign-off rules for medical supplies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to prepare properly. At work I'd say we should write a plan and train people. With friends I'd say the sooner people start, the better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel less rushed and more focused. I think I could be a compliance specialist by 2028, and that would stand up in 2031 better than a junior buyer's job. But I'd still expect the number of roles to shrink, so I wouldn't rely on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the medical device certificate in two years and ask for a move to regulatory affairs. I'd learn the AI tools well enough to teach others. I'd also pay down the mortgage with any bonus, aiming to lower the monthly payment, and keep six months of money as a safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels workable. Worried, yes, but with a to-do list, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra three years compared with the two-year case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra three years let me finish the qualification and have a real role, not a panic move. In the two-year case I'd be applying for anything. Here I could choose a slightly better path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell Camille when she asks about the news?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Camille the truth in simple words, that computers are getting better at thinking jobs, and grown-ups are working out what to do. I'd say she should learn to ask good questions, because that's what people will still need. Then I'd ask her what she thinks, since she's eleven and has opinions.

say: I'd say five years is **long enough** to prepare properly.
I'd suggest we write a plan and train people.
think: I could be a **compliance specialist** by 2028, which stands up better than a junior buyer's job.
I'd still expect fewer roles overall.
do: Finish the **medical device certificate** in two years and ask for a regulatory affairs move.
Learn AI tools well enough to teach colleagues.
Use bonuses to lower the mortgage payment and hold six months' savings.
feel: Workable; worried but with a **to-do list**.
S3.quote: The extra three years let me finish the qualification and have a real role, not a panic move.
fieldNote: Time turns into a **qualification** and a real role, which is her measure of a good plan.
Wants to talk to her daughter honestly and ask for her opinion.

steps.text: Finish the medical device regulation certificate in two years
Learn the AI tools well enough to teach colleagues
Use bonuses to cut the mortgage payment and keep six months saved
Explain the change honestly to Camille and ask her views

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade lets everyone adapt, if they use it. At work I'd carry on and encourage others to train. I'd also say governments need to plan for the supply chain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel fairly comfortable. By 2036 I'd be 53 and Camille would be 21 and Adam 18, so my main worry is what the kids study and whether the mortgage is finished. I'd feel more uneasy than anxious, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and build up skills one step at a time. I'd finish the certificate, move into compliance, and use AI in my work as I go. I'd save for the kids' education and aim for a smaller mortgage, since a decade is long enough to make real progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels manageable. I'd still think about it, but I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. What's your biggest uncertainty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The biggest uncertainty is whether the rules about human sign-off change. If regulators drop them, a compliance role wouldn't be safe either. I'd keep an eye on that, and I'd move early if the signs showed up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your plans differ if Hassan's job changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Hassan's job changed, I'd need to rethink. Teaching is also thinking work, and it's the same date for us, but kids still need adults for a long time. If his school cut staff, I'd want my savings and my compliance qualification to carry us.

say: I'd say a decade lets everyone **adapt**, if they use it.
I'd tell governments to plan for medical supply chains.
think: I'd feel fairly comfortable, but I'd worry what the **kids study** and whether the mortgage is finished.
do: Finish the certificate and move into **compliance** one step at a time.
Use AI in my work as I go.
Save for the kids' education and shrink the mortgage.
feel: Manageable; I'd think about it but **sleep fine**.
S4.quote: The biggest uncertainty is whether the rules about human sign-off change. If regulators drop them, a compliance role wouldn't be safe either.
fieldNote: Her one uncertainty is the **sign-off rule**, which she says she would watch closely.
Considers her husband's teaching job and the household as a pair of incomes.

steps.text: Finish the certificate and move into the compliance team
Use AI in daily buying and record the savings
Save for Camille and Adam's education fund
Watch for changes to the human sign-off rules

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I wouldn't have the qualification yet, and Hassan and I would have a mortgage and two children. What would help is clear rules that keep humans in the loop for medical supplies, some paid retraining, and a company that tells us the plan early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people at the other end. When a care home says they're down to their last box of gloves, I want a person on the line who understands. That bit of the job matters to me more than I expected.

headlineQuote: When a care home says they're down to their last box of gloves, I want a person on the line who understands.
portrait: Yara, 43, is a **junior buyer** of medical supplies at Meridian, with a teacher husband, two children and a long mortgage.
She is careful and organised, uses AI now and then, and sees regulation as her best protection.
Her plan is to qualify in medical device regulation and move into compliance before the buying team shrinks.
She goes from calm in mild worlds to anxious when AGI is near, and asks for clear rules and early notice.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most, because she wouldn't yet hold the qualification.
whatWouldHelp: Rules keeping **humans in the loop** for medical supplies, paid retraining and early notice from Meridian.
